props.title: Wall Street

sections.content: Wall Street defined the excesses and moral bankruptcy of 1980s financial culture through Gordon Gekko's infamous "greed is good" mantra. Oliver Stone's searing critique pairs Michael Douglas's Oscar-winning performance as the ruthless corporate raider with Charlie Sheen's naive broker Bud Fox, creating a modern Faustian bargain. The film captures the intoxicating allure of wealth through cinematographer Robert Richardson's gleaming shots of Manhattan skyscrapers and luxurious penthouses, while exposing the human cost of unchecked capitalism.

sections.content: The financial thriller genre exploded after Wall Street, with films like Boiler Room (2000) directly referencing Gekko's influence on a generation of traders. Margin Call (2011) and The Big Short (2015) brought documentary-like precision to explaining complex financial concepts while maintaining dramatic tension. These films share DNA with Stone's original - ambitious young protagonists seduced by wealth, moral compromises in pursuit of profit, and the devastating ripple effects of market manipulation.

The visual language of financial cinema evolved from Wall Street's emphasis on imposing architecture and status symbols. American Psycho (2000) satirized the materialistic obsessions, while Inside Job (2010) used sleek graphics to decode the 2008 crash. Modern entries like Industry (2020) maintain the genre's core focus on power, corruption and class while updating the aesthetic for contemporary finance. SUBHEAD: The Human Cost of Greed

sections.content: Where Wall Street pioneered showing finance's personal toll through Bud Fox's family relationships, later films expanded this focus. Equity (2016) examines gender dynamics in banking, while 99 Homes (2014) shows predatory lending's impact on ordinary families. Too Big to Fail (2011) captures the panic of financial leaders trying to prevent global collapse, proving the genre can humanize even its villains.
